title: Nathan Fielder Drops Weird Trailer for Secret Elizabeth Holmes Doc ‘You Can See Everything’
description: For years, it’s been rumored that Nathan Fielder had been interviewing Theranos founder (and certified huckster) Elizabeth Holmes — including visiti
body:
For years, it’s been rumored that Nathan Fielder had been interviewing Theranos founder (and certified huckster) Elizabeth Holmes — including visiting her in prison — for a top-secret documentary.

	And on Sunday night, that documentary premiered at the Telluride Film Festival.

	Titled “You Can See Everything,” the film is billed as follows:


	Thirty-four days before she’s sent to prison, notorious Silicon Valley founder Elizabeth Holmes invites a skeptical film crew to document her every move. What begins as an intimate portrait of an enigmatic felon becomes a mind-bending three-year journey into the abyss. From boundary-pushing directors Nathan Fielder and Lance Oppenheim comes ‘You Can See Everything.’
	

	Fielder is, of course, the comedic force behind the hit series “Nathan For You” and “The Rehearsal,” while Oppenheim is the acclaimed documentary filmmaker behind “Some Kind of Heaven” and the recent Robert Pattinson-starring Chris Hansen film “Primetime,” which just premiered to raves in Venice. “You Can See Everything” is an A24 film that will hit theaters sometime in October, and the studio also dropped a teaser-trailer for the film to coincide with its secret screening at the Colorado film fest.



	The trailer sees Fielder and Holmes locking eyes intensely, sizing each other up.

	“I don’t have anything to deceive you on,” Holmes tells him. “Of course I’m not deceiving you. I’m engaging with you as a human being. Why would I deceive you? There’s no reason for me to do that.”
	

	“OK. Alright. OK, good chat,” Fielder replies, before adding, “You’re being real right now?”

	“I’m always being real,” she says.

schema.headline: Nathan Fielder Drops Weird Trailer for Secret Elizabeth Holmes Doc ‘You Can See Everything’

title: Tokyo Film Festival Adds Nippon Cinema Now Competition, Crosscut Asia+ Section, New Award Honoring Women in Film
description: The Tokyo International Film Festival will introduce two new competitive awards, a Southeast Asia-focused section and a prize honoring women in cine
body:
The Tokyo International Film Festival will introduce two new competitive awards, a Southeast Asia-focused section and a prize honoring women in cinema.

	The Nippon Cinema Now section will award a Best Film prize and a Special Jury Prize this year, with a jury combining Japanese and international industry figures. TIFF said the awards are meant to support Japanese filmmakers ranging from newcomers to veterans and connect their work with audiences abroad.
	

	In a statement, TIFF festival director Hisamatsu Takeo said: “Through the establishment of a new competition within the Nippon Cinema Now section, we will shine a spotlight on exceptional new Japanese talent and introduce them to the world. We hope to give creators the courage to take on their next challenge while empowering them to advance to the global stage.”


	TIFF is also launching Crosscut Asia+, a new section developed with the Japan Foundation that continues the mission of the earlier Crosscut Asia strand, which ran from 2014 to 2019. The section will pair film programmers from Japan and Southeast Asia each year around a shared theme, with curators from both sides selecting the lineup together.

	The inaugural edition, themed Side by Side, was programmed by Raslene, who works as a film programmer and visual artist in Jakarta, and Ueda Masayuki, program director at the Tokyo repertory venue Waseda Shochiku, with Markus Nornes, professor emeritus at the University of Michigan, serving as advisor. Six films make up the initial slate: Rafael Manuel’s “Filipiñana,” Kamila Andini’s “Four Seasons in Java,” Polen Ly’s “Becoming Human,” Bachtiar Siagian’s 1957 film “Turang,” Daniel Hui’s “Small Hours of the Night” and Hafiz Rancajale’s “Behind the Flickering Light: The Archive.” Screenings will be accompanied by panel discussions organized by the two programmers.
	

	The festival’s third new initiative is the Kawakita Kashiko Award, established by the Kawakita Memorial Film Institute to honor women advancing film culture in Japan and internationally. The award takes its name from Kawakita Kashiko, known as “Madame Kawakita,” who introduced European films to Japanese audiences before and after World War II and was among those instrumental in establishing the Japan Film Library Council, an effort that eventually led to the creation of Japan’s National Film Archive. A committee of women selects the recipient, and the award will be presented as part of TIFF’s Women’s Empowerment section.

	Film critic Hata Sahoko is the award’s first recipient. Hata, who was born in Tokyo in 1931, moved to France as a journalist in 1957 before returning to Japan to join the distribution firm Shingaiei Haikyu Co., Ltd., then relocated to France as an acquisitions executive. She brought Jacques Tati’s “Mon Oncle” to Japan as her first major acquisition, followed by Jean-Luc Godard’s “Breathless” and René Clément’s “Purple Noon.” She has also authored several books and won the Japan Film Pen Club Award for her 2012 autobiographical novel “Kage no Bubun.”

	Hata said she initially declined the honor, recalling the prewar and postwar eras when women were largely excluded from the industry even as Kawakita built a career shaping which films crossed borders.

	“Her legacy remains a page in film history, as well as a chapter in the history of women,” Hata said. “On one occasion, Mme. Kawakita whispered to me: ‘As women, there are so many moments where we must endure, aren’t there?’ They were profound words indeed. It is precisely because I felt a compelling desire to pass this story on that I resolved to accept the award.”

	The selection committee for the inaugural Kashiko Kawakita Award comprises Sakano Yuka, executive director of the Kawakita Memorial Film Institute; Yamasaki Toshi, CEO and president of Toho-Towa Company, Limited; and Onda Yasuko, senior writer at the Yomiuri Shimbun.

	The 39th Tokyo International Film Festival runs Oct. 26–Nov. 4 and is hosted by Unijapan. The festival’s industry market, TIFFCOM, runs Oct. 28–30 and is organized by Japan’s Ministry of Economy, Trade and Industry, the Ministry of Internal Affairs and Communications, and Unijapan.

title: David Harbour Wins Emmy for Supporting Actor in Limited Series for ‘DTF: St. Louis’
description: David Harbour has won the Emmy for Supporting Actor in a Limited or Anthology Series or Movie for his portrayal of Floyd Smernitch in HBO Max’s “DTF
body:
David Harbour has won the Emmy for Supporting Actor in a Limited or Anthology Series or Movie for his portrayal of Floyd Smernitch in HBO Max’s “DTF St. Louis.” This marks the actor’s first Emmy win.

	As an executive producer on the series, he is also up for Outstanding Limited or Anthology Series for “DTF St. Louis,” which will be presented during next week’s Primetime Emmy Awards.

	Despite the first-time win, Harbour is no stranger to the Emmys, having received Supporting Actor nominations in both 2017 and 2018 for his role as Jim Hopper in “Stranger Things.”
	

	Harbour’s win came on night 2 of the Creative Arts Emmys.


	During his speech on stage, Harbour said he was really moved by the recognition. He said, “I can’t believe that you’ve embraced our show so much this beautiful, vulnerable, weird show that I love so much.” He went on to say, “In terms of my fellow nominees, it was not a fair fight. I got to play Floyd Smernitch, who is an incredibly written character by a genius named named Steve Conrad, who,  is a true original.” Harbour concluded his speech by thanking the team at HBO and said, “Everybody was nominated for my show. It’s unbelievable.”

	Last month, Harbour spoke to Variety about the difference between then and now: “Back then it was pretty singular, focused on you as an actor,” he says of his 2017 nominations for “Stranger Things.” “Going into this, it’s the show. It’s every single actor. ‘Stranger Things’ wasn’t mine. I was jobbed in,” he said. “I feel so proud. It’s my baby.”

	His fellow nominees included Jason Bateman (“DTF St. Louis”), Richard Gadd (“Half Man), Richard Jenkins (“DTF St. Louis), Charles Melton (“Beef”) and Nick Offerman (“Death by Lightning”).
	

	“DTF St. Louis” debuted on HBO Max in March and was well received by audiences and critics alike. The show has racked up 13 Emmy nominations this season, including Limited or Anthology Series, Casting for a Limited or Anthology Series or Movie and Directing for a Limited or Anthology Series or Movie.

title: Hong Sangsoo’s Locarno Winner ‘Nowhere to Lay My Eyes’ Anchors Wave of Sales Deals for Finecut Ahead of Toronto
description: Korean sales house Finecut has closed a string of international deals for three festival titles, including Hong Sangsoo‘s Locarno prizewinner “Nowhe
body:
Korean sales house Finecut has closed a string of international deals for three festival titles, including Hong Sangsoo‘s Locarno prizewinner “Nowhere to Lay My Eyes,” ahead of the Toronto Film Festival.

	The film marks Hong’s 35th feature. It competed in the Concorso Internazionale at the 79th Locarno Film Festival and picked up three awards: the Pardo for Best Direction, the Pardo for Best Performance and the Ecumenical Jury Prize.
	

	Finecut has sold the film to North America (the Cinema Guild), the U.K. (Institute of Contemporary Arts), Spain (Atalante), China (Hugoeast), Austria (Filmgarten) and Taiwan (Cola Films). The story follows a woman who, after 10 years apart, visits her mother together with her brother and spends two days with her mother’s new family.


	Also among the deals is “Long Long Night,” a 3D animated feature marking the directorial debut of Youm Kyu Bock. The film has been pre-sold to Japan’s Geek Pictures Inc. ahead of its world premiere at Toronto, where it screens in the Centrepiece selection. From there, it moves on to the Busan International Film Festival‘s competition lineup, then to the Sitges Film Festival, where it competes in the Anima’t section.

	The film adapts a bestselling Korean novel based on a true story that has sold more than 800,000 copies and was named to the International Youth Library’s 2021 White Ravens list in Munich.

	“Even from just the 15-minute promo footage, we were deeply moved by the beauty of the film and the way it captures the world of the original story, by the endearing bond between the last rhino on Earth and a penguin, and by the kindness and strength that come through in its message of living for someone else. We immediately felt that this was a film we wanted to bring to audiences in Japan,” said Kosano Tamotsu, CEO of Geek Pictures Inc.
	

	Rounding out the slate is “Dora,” the third feature from director July Jung, which premiered in the Directors’ Fortnight at Cannes, and Busan International Film Festival has selected it for its Gala presentation lineup. Finecut has closed deals for the film in Japan (Geek Pictures Inc.) and Taiwan (Light Year Images).

	Jung is the first Korean female director to have three consecutive features selected for Cannes. “Dora” pairs rising Korean actress Kim Doyeon in the title role with Japanese actress Ando Sakura, known for “Godzilla Minus One,” “Monster” and the Palme d’Or winner “Shoplifters.”

	During Toronto, Finecut will also introduce the animated adventure “Guardians of the Video Game,” based on a webtoon with 345 million views worldwide, and “Wash Away,” a Japanese horror-thriller about a couple whose lakeside retreat turns sinister amid a resort’s belief that its waters can cleanse the soul.

	Miyahara’s short film “Suck” was selected for the Clermont-Ferrand International Short Film Festival, and “Wash Away” marks his feature debut, premiering in the Sitges Film Festival’s Panorama section.

title: John Turturro Has Waited 40 Years for an Oscar Nomination. ‘The Only Living Pickpocket in New York’ Makes the Case
description: Forty years into a career that has made him one of American cinema’s most recognizable character actors, John Turturro has a Cannes best actor prize
body:
Forty years into a career that has made him one of American cinema’s most recognizable character actors, John Turturro has a Cannes best actor prize, an enviable résumé and exactly zero Oscar mornings when his name was read aloud with the words “and the nominees are.”

	Sony Pictures Classics is determined to end the drought with his work in the acclaimed “The Only Living Pickpocket in New York,” which premiered at Sundance last January and made its fall festival bow at Telluride this weekend, where the film and Turturro’s invigorating turn as an aging pickpocket are drawing acclaim.
	

	Turturro, 69, has been making the rounds in the Colorado mountains, attending Q&As and a Saturday night dinner hosted by Sony Pictures Classics, where writer-director Noah Segan mingled with press and industry attendees.


	Turturro has spent four decades operating in the space reserved for actors everyone recognizes and almost nobody thinks of as an Oscar nominee. He has worked with masters of cinema such as the Coen brothers, Spike Lee and Robert Redford and has appeared opposite everyone from Tom Hanks to Adam Sandler. He’s played gangsters, professors, detectives, eccentrics, husbands, fathers and men who seem to have wandered into the wrong movie and somehow made it better.

	And yet, the Academy has never invited him to the party.

	And it’s not like he hasn’t been close. Turturro won best actor at Cannes for the Coen brothers’ “Barton Fink” in 1991. Three years later, his combustible Herbie Stempel in Robert Redford’s “Quiz Show” collected Golden Globe and SAG Award nominations, the kind of precursor support that usually precedes an Oscar bid. But each time, the industry seemed to look elsewhere.
	

	The television world has been kinder. His weary defense attorney in “The Night Of,” HBO’s 2016 crime drama, drew Emmy, Golden Globe and SAG Award nominations. His tender, unraveling Irving Bailiff on “Severance,” Apple TV’s dystopian workplace thriller, has since earned him two Emmy nominations, the most recent lost to his own castmate Tramell Tillman in 2025.

	“The Only Living Pickpocket in New York” can change that.



	

	



	In a similar vein to Richard Jenkins’ first career nomination for the 2007 drama “The Visitor,” Turturro can be the overdue veteran to finally see his name in lights. Segan’s Sundance breakout, acquired by SPC for a fall release, gives Turturro something four decades of great supporting performances never could: a movie that he leads, one that lives and dies on him.

	He plays Harry Lehman, an analog thief operating in a city where the very concept of pickpocketing has become obsolete. Wallets increasingly contain less cash, phones have replaced maps and tickets and two-factor authentication has made the modern world almost aggressively hostile to the old-fashioned criminal. Harry is clinging to a disappearing profession while caring for his ailing wife, Rosie.

	While that metaphor is hardly subtle, it’s also part of its appeal. Harry is not simply a thief whose trade is dying; he’s a man confronting his own obsolescence.

	SPC calls it the finest performance of Turturro’s career. Distributor hyperbole is usually best treated as campaign copy. But here, it resonates. Turturro has never been an actor who needed to announce himself. He slips into other people’s scenes, finds the detail nobody else thought to play and then, almost imperceptibly, becomes the most interesting person in the room. The Academy has rewarded that instinct repeatedly, just not when Turturro has been the person standing at the center of the frame.

	As an awards campaign, the studio is following a familiar formula: a beloved, never-nominated veteran finally gets a leading role worthy of his gifts. But the strongest version of the pitch is not “Give John Turturro an Oscar.” It is “Look at what John Turturro has been doing all along.”

	The Academy has historically responded to overdue narratives, particularly when the performance provides a credible reason to act on the sentiment. Turturro has the résumé, the festival pedigree and the late-career showcase that can turn years of admiration into a voting impulse.
	

	“The Only Living Pickpocket in New York” is a movie about a man whose skills belong to another era, trying to prove they still have value. The meta-text is impossible to miss. Turturro’s awards case makes essentially the same argument about the actor himself.

	It also helps to have Steve Buscemi in the cast, who could mount his own first awards run for “Wild Horse Nine,” along with the best awards campaigner this side of the sun, Jamie Lee Curtis, who delivers a killer one-scene wonder.

	Like a lot of SPC films, neither the movie nor Turturro may seem the loudest voice in the room right now and plenty of pundits will write it off early, especially once precursors start rolling in. But as the studio has shown with titles like “The Father,” “Parallel Mothers” and “I’m Still Here,” the ground game and striking when it matters most, is what wins these campaigns.

	And Turturro may not even be the film’s only awards story. Segan, long a familiar face in front of the camera, wrote and directed “The Only Living Pickpocket in New York” himself and a spare, mournful original like this one is exactly the kind of writer-director calling card the original screenplay race tends to reward. It happens more than voters remember. “Frozen River,” another SPC sleeper, paired Melissa Leo’s lead nomination with a surprise original screenplay nod for writer-director Courtney Hunt and “Nebraska” did the same for Bruce Dern and scribe Bob Nelson. If the film connects with voters, Segan’s script could ride in alongside its star.

	The best actor field, notably, is shaping up to be incredibly crowded. Heading into the fall festivals, pundits had already penciled in the likes of Matt Damon (“The Odyssey”), Ryan Gosling (“Project Hail Mary”) and Sebastian Stan (“Fjord”), and Venice and Telluride added John Malkovich (“Wild Horse Nine”) and Andrew Scott (“Elsinore”) to the conversation. SPC will have to make noise without overselling a performance whose appeal lies in its subtlety. But if the campaign can persuade voters to see Harry not as a novelty but as the culmination of everything Turturro has spent a career doing, the narrative becomes difficult to ignore.

	Let’s see if this pickpocket can steal some hearts along the way.

schema.headline: John Turturro Has Waited 40 Years for an Oscar Nomination. ‘The Only Living Pickpocket in New York’ Makes the Case

title: ‘Woman Unknown’ Review: Some More Problematic Sex — and Its Consequences — by Denmark’s May el-Toukhy
description: Against the rubble gray and stiff mahogany with which director May el-Toukhy washes out her post-Second World War Copenhagen, the pops of crimson in
body:
Against the rubble gray and stiff mahogany with which director May el-Toukhy washes out her post-Second World War Copenhagen, the pops of crimson in “Woman Unknown” announce a stark symbolism that’s about as subtle as the red swastika eventually smeared on the front door of protagonist Marie (Mathilde Arcel). As obvious as these subliminal scarlet letters may be, they’re not without a certain Hitchcockian power in a film about sexual shame and a kind of violence against women’s bodies that operates from the inside out. But as this is el-Toukhy — whose steely 2019 incest drama “Queen of Hearts” was promptly adapted by French provocatrice Catherine Breillat in “Last Summer” — the film’s feminism, or lack thereof depending on how you take your empowerment, is a prickly matter by design. 
	

	As with the women played by Emmanuelle Riva in “Hiroshima, Mon Amour” or Charlotte Rampling in “The Night Porter,” a crisis is sparked over Marie’s supposedly soiled sheets, with el-Toukhy basing her story on the many accounts of public punishment received by women from Nazi-occupied countries who had sexual relations with German soldiers during the war. It’s a spicy conceit from the only woman director in Venice’s main competition, and its implications arguably creep out beyond the historical context in question — should our private lives be judged and exposed to real consequences? Not that el-Toukhy has made a particularly open film with this neatly scripted psychodrama, her austere visuals and prim haut-bourgeois setting practically asking to be unraveled. 
	

	Marie, a maid and nanny to the twiggy blonde child of her employer Christian (Carsten Bjornlund), a widower and owner of a glove-making factory, carries herself as if permanently bound in a corset: breath held, mouth tight, her eyes shifty as if dreading the next reprimand. It makes sense given her workplace’s exacting standards, in which place settings are arranged according to centimeter-precise measurements and stony head maid Esther (Marina Bouras) is always watching. 

	But early on, when Christian discreetly caresses Marie’s cheek, it’s clear that it’s not just her job that’s at stake should she fall, but her newly gained status as lady of the house. A long shot of a pearly silk dress — a wedding dress — dangling like a carrot in an empty closet doubles as a harbinger of doom when she’s spotted by Karl (Thorbjorn Hedegaard), an old classmate from her hometown who’s much too eager to catch up. It’s through this jittery encounter, and a visit to the doctor where Marie re-ups on the liquid opium she takes to dull the pain of sex with Christian, that we learn she once had a baby boy, and that child caused her to flee her past life. 

	El-Toukhy and Maren Louise Kaehne’s script doesn’t connect the dots for you with explanatory dialogue, but those dots are still awfully close. Scenes of nameless women being knocked around on the streets by gangs of men, who chop off their hair and tear off their clothes before branding them with painted swastikas, make it brutally clear what Marie is hiding from. And what starts out with the echoing, empty rooms of paranoia turns into whispers from the domestic staff after Karl discovers where Marie lives. The building door is marked with Nazi insignia shortly after, leaving Marie desperate to cover the tracks that lead to her. 

	Cinematographer Jasper Spanning’s static, shadowy frames give way to shallow-lensed close-ups as Marie plunges into a panicked spiral that, at one point, sees her consenting to a wad of spit in her mouth. That scene, which begins with a pan over Marie’s naked body as Karl swats her hands away to do as he pleases, rhymes with comparably frigid moments involving the gilded milieu she aspires to join — as when a snooty tailor takes her measurements or when Christian uses her as a hand model to show off a new glove design. This body does not belong to her, and her refusal to cede control of it to her male masters will end in their wrath, a point made repeatedly, albeit with a harrowing range of registers. 
	

	Marie’s humanity and capacity for tenderness come through in her scenes with children, though these aren’t nearly weighty enough — despite Arcel’s commendably nervy performance —  to carry out her concluding crash-out convincingly. Her relationship with the next-door neighbor, a single mother far too liberated to escape scrutiny in midcentury Denmark, gets a few threadbare scenes to prime this spiritual flurry, where red appears one last time in the form of blood on Marie’s hands. Worse than the loogie is the feminine betrayal that weighs on her soul, or at least that’s how it’s supposed to read.

schema.headline: ‘Woman Unknown’ Review: Some More Problematic Sex — and Its Consequences — by Denmark’s May el-Toukhy

title: Andy ‘The Butcher’ Williams, Musician and Wrestler, Dies After Match
description: Andy “The Butcher” Williams, a professional wrestler who played guitar with the bands Every Time I Die and Atomic Rule, died Saturday night after co
body:
Andy “The Butcher” Williams, a professional wrestler who played guitar with the bands Every Time I Die and Atomic Rule, died Saturday night after collapsing at the end of his match in Millvale, Pennsylvania. He was 48.

	Williams was rushed to the hospital but did not survive. The rest of the match was called off after the medical emergency.

	His most recent promoter All Elite Wrestling released a statement, saying “All Elite Wrestling is saddened to learn of the passing of Andy Williams, aka The Butcher. A trailblazing musician with ETID and Atomic Rule, Williams made a successful transition into the world of professional wrestling and was incredibly respected by his peers both in and out of the ring. Our condolences go out to Williams’ family, friends and fans.”
	

	Williams had been competing alongside his tag-team partner Jesse Guilmette, “The Blade” at Enjoy Wrestling’s Five Years event. 


	The New York native co-founded the Buffalo, N.Y. metalcore band Every Time I Die in 1998, and the group released nine albums before splitting up in 2022. His new band Atomic Rule was set to tour the West Coast in November with GWAR, and earlier on Saturday he had posted, “Update of the work we’ve been putting in! So stoked to share all this with you! We feel like we’ve finally found our feet planted to this beautiful earth and now we’re running full speed!”

	He started wrestling on the independent circuit in 2015 at the age of 37, and joined All Elite Wrestling in 2019, performing as the Butcher. Williams and Guilmette’s contracts with All Elite expired in June, and they returned to  independent wrestling.

title: Macklemore Calls Out ‘Free Palestine’ Onstage, Spurring Petition Demanding He Leave Ed Sheeran Tour
description: Macklemore opened for Ed Sheeran on Friday night in New Jersey at the MetLife Stadium, and during his set the rapper sang out “Free Palestine” befor
body:
Macklemore opened for Ed Sheeran on Friday night in New Jersey at the MetLife Stadium, and during his set the rapper sang out “Free Palestine” before launching into a speech, telling the audience he wanted people in Gaza and the occupied West Bank to know they had not been forgotten. 

	“I believe that every human being walking on this earth deserves exactly the same freedom,” he said. He repeated the remarks during Saturday night’s performance. 
	

	His politically-themed set sparked a petition from the Israeli American Council, which demanded the rapper be removed from the remaining dates on the Loop tour.


	The petition, which does not show how many signatures it has gathered, reads “This was an Ed Sheeran concert – not a political rally, not a protest, and not an activist event. The issue is not whether Macklemore has the right to hold political views. The question is where the line should be drawn when an opening act uses a global concert platform to advance a one-sided political agenda.”

	Macklemore also called out U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement during his remarks. He released the song “Hind’s Hall,” which criticizes Israel’s actions in Gaza, in 2024 and has directed proceeds from the song to go to humanitarian efforts from the UNRWA. 

	On social media, some concertgoers said they walked out because they had not expected a ‘political rally,” accusing Macklemore of antisemitism. Others applauded his remarks, writing “Music has always been a vital platform for human rights advocacy, not just mindless escape.”

schema.headline: Macklemore Calls Out ‘Free Palestine’ Onstage, Spurring Petition Demanding He Leave Ed Sheeran Tour

title: Netflix Bets ‘Ink’ and Its Timely Rupert Murdoch Story Can Win Oscars for Danny Boyle and Guy Pearce
description:
Netflix wants the “ink” to dry on its Oscar prospects.

	Danny Boyle made his first trip to Venice with “Ink,” his adaptation of James Graham’s stag
body:
Netflix wants the “ink” to dry on its Oscar prospects.

	Danny Boyle made his first trip to Venice with “Ink,” his adaptation of James Graham’s stage sensation, which opened the 83rd edition in competition before moving through Telluride and Toronto, with the streamer giving it a December theatrical release and a January streaming date.

	The early temperature is reading warm. “Ink” drew a four-minute standing ovation on opening night in Venice, and the reactions filtering out of Telluride have been buzzing across the mountains, the kind of enthusiasm and respect a Netflix campaign is built to amplify.
	

	The subject is an origin myth of modern media: Rupert Murdoch’s 1969 acquisition of a dying tabloid called The Sun and the rapid transformation that followed. Graham, adapting his own Tony-nominated play, approaches the story with the mechanics of a heist. Boyle supplies the velocity.


	The central question is not simply how Murdoch built a newspaper. It is how two men helped invent the modern attention economy that shapes all of our lives today.

	Guy Pearce plays a brash, thirty-something Murdoch, an outsider with a chip on his shoulder and a plan for disrupting Fleet Street. Jack O’Connell plays editor Larry Lamb, the working-class newspaperman Murdoch pushes past every line the establishment believes cannot be crossed.

	Both actors have obvious awards narratives, but two very different categories to break into.

	Pearce arrives two years after his first Oscar nomination, a supporting actor bid for “The Brutalist,” which gives him the benefit of recent Academy recognition. And the role could hardly be more of the moment. Murdoch is a figure many hold responsible for the fractured, combustible information environment the U.S. is living through right now and there is a particular charge in watching an actor humanize the young man who lit the fuse. That timeliness is the kind of thing that fuels an Oscar campaign.
	

	O’Connell arrives with something different: momentum. Between “Sinners” and the “28 Years Later” films, he is coming off a stretch that has significantly raised his visibility. Being a hot commodity right now, and perhaps even a package deal with Pearce in voters’ minds, could give him a fighting shot in a very crowded best actor field.

	We have seen roles like Pearce’s cakewalk to nominations before, purely on the nature of the part, even when pundits wrote them off early. Look at the run of real-life figures who landed supporting bids: Jon Voight in “Ali” (2001), Matt Damon in “Invictus” (2009), Kenneth Branagh in “My Week with Marilyn” (2011), Christopher Plummer in “All the Money in the World” (2017), Sam Rockwell in “Vice” (2018), J.K. Simmons in “Being the Ricardos” (2021) and Jeremy Strong in “The Apprentice” (2024).

	Pearce may not have the most screen time, but he is memorable in every frame. O’Connell has the more obvious breakout narrative and, as the story’s beating heart, the showier dramatic arc.

	Two performances from one film can coexist comfortably in an awards campaign, but they can also create a strategic problem. The distributor must establish why both actors are essential without letting voters perceive one as stealing oxygen from the other.



	

					Guy Pearce as Rupert Murdoch and Jack O’Connell as Larry Lamb in “Ink”
									Netflix
	



	There is also a screenplay story here, and a recent precedent worth studying.

	Graham is adapting his own acclaimed play, which puts “Ink” in the adapted screenplay conversation and on a path that “One Night in Miami” walked in 2020. That film, too, launched at Venice and Kemp Powers turned his own stage work into an adapted screenplay nomination while the movie also landed an acting nod for Leslie Odom Jr. A playwright translating his own material, a festival launch and a performance the industry embraces: the template is right there.

	But Netflix will look to check even more boxes.

	Beyond the two actors, “Ink” is built to contend in the crafts. Its production design, by Carson McColl and Gareth Pugh, rebuilds a vanished Fleet Street. Fin Oates cuts the film with a fragmented, kinetic energy that recalls the associative style Hank Corwin brought to Adam McKay’s “The Big Short” and “Vice.” Johnnie Burn, the Oscar-winning sound designer of “The Zone of Interest,” lends the film one of the most decorated ears in the business. And composer Daniel Pemberton supplies an original score with the propulsion Boyle’s movies demand, capping a bombastic year that also includes “Project Hail Mary.”
	

	Netflix has the resources to make all of those cases.

	The larger question is whether the company has the bandwidth. Its fall slate is stacked, with “La Bola Negra,” “The Adventures of Cliff Booth,” “Possible Love,” “Gentle Monster” and “The Mosquito Bowl” all angling for the same oxygen. “Ink” will have to compete not only against rival distributors but against Netflix’s own contenders for screeners, headlines, events, Q & As and voter attention. The Venice-Telluride-Toronto sequence helps enormously, giving the movie the sort of early critical footprint that can turn an awards campaign into a sustained conversation.

	And Boyle’s presence adds another narrative. As the Oscar-winning filmmaker behind “Slumdog Millionaire,” he brings such a distinctive visual and kinetic signature that the fall circuit was an obvious place for the film to bow.

	The James Graham connection gives “Ink” a larger cultural context. His work has repeatedly mined the intersection of power, institutions and public life, from politics to journalism. “Ink” arrives in a media environment in which the questions surrounding Murdoch’s influence feel less like history than an origin story for the world audiences inhabit now.

	That resonance is the film’s best weapon, and the campaign will not have to manufacture it.

	“Ink” argues that we are all still living in the paper they printed.

	Midway through Night 2 of the 78th Emmys, there’s a surprising series leader: Prime Video’s “Spider-Noir,” which has taken home five Emmys just days after learning that the show had been canceled and wouldn’t return for a second season. Despite that, the stunt team from the show won for stunt performance, while the series also won for sound editing for a comedy or drama series (one hour), title design, special visual effects in a single episode and cinematography for a series (one hour).
	

	Speaking about the cancelation of the show while having a triumphant moment at the Emmys, supervising stunt coordinator Freddy Bouciegues said, “I’m excited because we got to do a cool show. We got to do some big action. We got to do everything we wanted. Our showrunners let us let the stunt team. We came to the table with ideas. They said, ‘Yes, run with it,’ and we got to do everything we wanted.” Added stunt coordinator Hugh Aodh O’Brien: “I’m happy we got the win, and that’s, I guess the icing on the cake.” 


	The Sunday ceremony included 53 categories mostly focused in the scripted arena (Night 1 was centered on unscripted categories). Among the key races are the guest star categories in both comedy and drama, as well as animated program, cinematography, character voice-over, stunt performance, costumes and makeup.

	RELATED: Bad Bunny ‘Super Bowl Halftime Show,’ ‘Muppets’ and ‘Traitors’ Win Night 1 Creative Arts Emmy Awards

	But perhaps the most anticipated categories of the night come with a bit of controversy: In order to free up time during NBC’s Emmys ceremony on Sept. 14, five categories originally expected to be passed out during the telecast were instead moved to tonight. That includes writing for a variety series, supporting actor and actress in a limited/anthology series or movie, directing for a limited series/anthology or movie and writing for a limited series/anthology or movie.
	

	Meanwhile, with so many major awards switching to what has traditionally been known as the “Creative Arts Emmys,” the TV Academy also dropped the “Creative Arts” distinction for the Sept. 5 and Sept. 6 ceremonies — and now refers to all three events (including the Sept. 14 telecast) as simply the “Emmys.”

	“Paradise” star Shailene Woodley won for guest actress in a drama series. Speaking about her win, Woodley told members of the press, “I’m a fan of the show and I’m a small piece of it and I feel very excited to be on board their bigger mission and to have my little slice of the pie and contribute what I was able to contribute.” She added, “I think that the show is so dynamic in its range, and the fact that it’s a sci-fi show that brings so much humanity and art to the genre is really unparalleled.” 

	Also, Julie Andrews won her fourth Emmy, landing the award in the character voice-over performance category. This was her second win in the category. The first time around, Andrews made history as the oldest woman ever to win at age 89. At 90, she extended her own record at the ceremony. 

	Also on Sunday, the Television Academy handed out its first-ever “Legacy Award,” given to “I Love Lucy” — the series that set the blueprint for sitcoms and created the template for TV syndication. As announced in January, the new Legacy Award was created to recognize television programs “that have made a profound and lasting impact on audiences and remain relevant to society, culture and the industry.” The org’s Special Awards committee (formerly known as the Governors Award committee) selects candidates for the Legacy Award annually, and then the Board of Governors votes on the entries.

	“Lucy’s electric energy and elastic physicality didn’t just influence me, it became a part of me,” said June Diane Raphael (“The Morning Show”), who introduced the honor. “.Without Lucy we don’t have Carol Burnett, Tina Fey or Kristen Wiig. Lucy’s performances were all so vanity free. What could be more beautiful.”

	Bringing production back to Los Angeles was a theme among the artisans throughout the evening. “Palm Royale” costume designer Alix Friedberg praised her team. She said, “This show was built with the hands of the most incredibly talented costume teams, textile artists, and builders based in the great city of L.A.” 
	

	She was one of the many winners of the night to give a shout out to Los Angeles. Similarly, “The Pitt” casting director Cathy Sandrich Gelfond spoke backstage and about working in the city. She said, “We’re so happy to give all these actors jobs and bring work back to L.A.” 

	“Fallout” costume designer Dayna Pink, who won the outstanding fantasy/sci-fi costumes category, also praised the Prime Video show which shot season 2 in the city. Speaking backstage, Pink said it was great to shoot in Los Angeles because of all the resources in the city. 

	“The rental houses are here. We have great crews here, and supporting this city in particular, spreads out,” she said. “It isn’t just the costumes, but the more people that are here, the more businesses we can help along, because this business has had a tough time.” She added, “I’m really proud to be part of something that’s shooting in California and how important it is for Jonathan Nolan to make that happen.”

	Prime Video’s “Spider-Noir” took home five Emmys just days after learning that the show had been canceled and wouldn’t return for a second season. Despite that, the stunt team from the show won for stunt performance, while the series also won for sound editing for a comedy or drama series (one hour), title design, special visual effects in a single episode and cinematography for a series (one hour). 

	Meanwhile, on Saturday’s Night 1, “The Apple Music Super Bowl LX Halftime Show Starring Bad Bunny” led the pack with seven Emmys, including a win for the singer himself. It won for outstanding choreography for variety or reality programming (Charm La’Donna, Karina Ortiz), outstanding production design for a variety special Bruce Rodgers), outstanding music direction (Miguel Gandelman) and outstanding variety special (live). That was followed by Peacock’s “The Traitors,” which won six.

Egyptian TV Host

body:
Egyptian TV Host
                          Sentenced to Death by Hanging for Drug Trafficking
                      
                  
                                                                        Published 
                              September 6, 2026
                            5:45 PM PDT
                                                                            
      
    
                  
          
                          
                
                                  
      
    
            An Egyptian TV host broke down in tears in court after learning her fate in a massive drug trafficking case ... death by hanging.
      
    
            Sarah Khalifa, a 39-year-old former host of the Egyptian crime show "Mission Impossible," was sentenced to death in Cairo after being convicted of helping run an organized drug operation.
      
    
                  
          
                          
                
                                  
      
    
            She and 11 others were sentenced to death after prosecutors accused the group of importing raw materials used to manufacture synthetic drugs and storing the finished product inside residential homes.
      

            Khalifa reportedly sobbed as the sentence was handed down, pleading with the court and insisting she didn't need money from drugs. She denies the allegations, reportedly telling investigators she'd never even smoked a cigarette.
      
    
                  
          
                          
                
                                  
      
    
            Authorities say the sprawling case involved 28 defendants and led to the seizure of more than 1,600 pounds of narcotics, along with unlicensed guns and ammunition.
      
    
            Nine other defendants were sentenced to life in prison, while seven were acquitted.
      
    
            Khalifa -- who also ran a cosmetic surgery clinic and an event-planning company -- was arrested in 2025.
      
    
            The death sentence was issued after the court consulted Egypt's grand mufti, a required step in Egyptian capital cases ... and the ruling can still be appealed.

                          Facing Calls to Boot Him From Ed Sheeran Tour
body:
Macklemore
                          Facing Calls to Boot Him From Ed Sheeran Tour
                      
                  
                                                                        Published 
                              September 6, 2026
                            5:15 PM PDT
                                                                            
      
    
                  
          
                          
                
                  
      
    
            Macklemore is catching serious heat for turning his opening set on Ed Sheeran's tour into a political statement ... and now an Israeli-American group wants him booted from the remaining shows.
      
    
            The "Thrift Shop" rapper opened for Ed Friday and Saturday at MetLife Stadium in New Jersey, where he used part of his set to voice support for Palestinians and rip Israel's conduct in Gaza.
      
    
        Waiting for your permission to load the Twitter Tweet.
      
    
            Macklemore repeatedly shouted "Free Palestine" and performed his 2024 protest track "Hind's Hall" as images tied to Gaza and pro-Palestinian demonstrations flashed behind him.
      

            That didn't sit well with the Israeli-American Council, which has launched a petition calling on Sheeran and tour organizers to dump Macklemore from the rest of the "Loop" tour ... arguing fans paid for a concert, not a political rally.
      
    
            The petition does not publicly show how many signatures it has collected.
      
    
                  
          
                          
                
                  
      
    
            The reaction online has been predictably fiery ... with some concertgoers saying they walked out and accusing Macklemore of pushing antisemitic rhetoric, while others defended his decision to use the stage to speak about the war.
      
    
            As TMZ has previously reported ... Macklemore has been outspoken on the Israel-Palestine conflict for years.
      
    
            Back in 2024, singer-songwriter Matisyahu ripped "Hind's Hall" as antisemitic ... telling TMZ he believed the song was only making an already ugly divide worse.
      
    
            Macklemore also sparked outrage that same year when he chanted "f*** America" during a pro-Palestinian festival in Seattle.

body:
Lincoln Memorial Reflecting Pool
                          One Mess After Another Since Makeover
                      
      
    
                  
          
                          
                
                  
      
    
            The Lincoln Memorial Reflecting Pool is looking rough again ... after powerful storms turned the already-troubled tourist attraction into an even bigger mess.
      
    
        Waiting for your permission to load the Twitter Tweet.
      
    
            Fencing and black tarp surrounding the closed-off pool have toppled over, mucking up the view ... with parts of the barrier spilling into the water and leaving the area looking battered and disheveled.
      
    
                  
          
                          
                
                  
      
    
            Recent storms hammered D.C. with heavy rain and powerful winds ... knocking down trees and sending debris flying across the District -- and the Reflecting Pool wasn't spared.
      

            Of course, it's just the latest headache for the famous landmark after its multimillion-dollar makeover became a months-long saga.
      
    
                  
          
                          
                
                  
      
    
            As TMZ previously reported ... the pool developed algae and its new blue coating began peeling shortly after the renovation. President Donald Trump blamed vandals for some of the damage, leading to arrests -- but prosecutors later dropped the felony case against former Olympian David Hearn after concluding the installation itself was flawed.
      
    
            Trump has continued insisting vandalism played a role ... and the administration recently shelled out more millions to tackle the pool's algae problem.
      
    
            So much for keeping up appearances ...
